results.content:
Auto-approves safe PRs. LiveReview approves the lowest-risk 30-50% of PRs under your policy; the rest go to a human. CodeRabbit offers this too, opt-in, when threads are resolved, checks pass, and risk is under your limit. Greptile's is beta, and only on a clean 5/5 review. SonarQube, Claude Code review, and Cursor Bugbot do not approve at all — a quality gate passes or fails, or a person has to click approve. Copilot has a public-preview approval, off by default, with undocumented criteria.
 Learns from your own production incidents and reverts. This is where LiveReview stands alone: every revert or incident retrains your organization's own model. None of the six alternatives are documented as feeding production outcomes back into the review itself. [...] The loop runs like this:

1. Track outcomes. Trace production incidents and rollbacks back to the commits and reviews behind them.
2. Learn from the data. Combine those outcomes with LLM analysis, static checks, and ML signals into one risk score per change.
3. Automate selectively. Auto-approve the lowest-risk 30-50% of changes. Choose a conservative, balanced, or aggressive policy. Risky or uncertain changes still go to a human.
4. Keep improving. Track incidents, false approvals, and overrides, and tighten or loosen the policy as real data comes in.

The result: your reviewers stop reading every line of every diff, and start spending their full attention on the 50-70% of changes that actually carry risk.

# Meet LiveReview: Auto Approve 30-50% of Your Low-Risk PRs, Safely

Earlier this year, we built a small tool called git-lrc.

It fixed one problem: engineers committing AI-written code they had not read. git-lrc put a review in front of every commit, right in the terminal. In February, it reached #3 Product of the Day on Product Hunt, and it now has 1.5k+ GitHub stars.

As teams adopted it, a bigger problem showed up one step later, at the pull request.

AI made code cheap to write. Review stayed expensive. [...] 8. Works with your git provider and your AI key  
GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Gitea, and Azure DevOps. Reuse the Claude or OpenAI key you already pay for, or any of 15+ AI providers, or use the LiveReview model.

9. Free and self-hostable  
Run it on your own infrastructure. No seats, no per-review bill that climbs as your team grows.

## Why this matters now

Most AI code review tools add more comments to the pull request. More comments is not the goal. Fewer incidents, fewer rollbacks, and less senior reviewer time are the goal.

LiveReview follows the approach behind Meta's internal AI review system, RADAR: score every change for risk, fast-track the safe ones, and route the risky ones to the right reviewers. At Meta, this approach led to:

Watch the demo: LiveReview auto-approving a low-risk change while routing a risky change to a human reviewer.

## LiveReview auto-approves your safest 30-50% of pull requests [...] Every pull request gets a risk score. The lowest-risk 30-50% are approved automatically. The rest go to the right human, in the right order, ranked by how much they actually matter.

## How LiveReview differs from other AI reviewers

Most tools in this space pick one of two jobs: find issues, or check style. LiveReview is built to be the layer that decides whether a human needs to look at all, and ranks what matters when they do.

Here is what actually changes when you compare LiveReview against CodeRabbit, Greptile, SonarQube, Claude Code review, GitHub Copilot review, and Cursor Bugbot, feature by feature, not by marketing claim: [...] Most of the alternatives find issues and leave the approval decision to a person. LiveReview makes the "does a human need to look at this at all" decision itself, backs it with your own production outcome data, and only then prioritizes what's left for the humans who do look. See the full feature-by-feature comparison for every row.

## The problem: reviews did not scale with AI

Most AI code review tools add more comments to the pull request. More comments is not the goal. Fewer incidents, fewer rollbacks, and less senior reviewer time are the goal. We measure LiveReview by production outcomes, not by comment count.

If your engineers produce PRs faster than they can review them, more AI coding tools will make it worse. Look at where time actually goes. For us, it was waiting for approval.

## Try it yourself

Start with the code review automation template, which runs on every PR opened across your configured projects and leaves structured review comments. The auto-approve layer is a policy decision on top of that: define your low-risk criteria, build the classification automation, and let the agent handle the rest.

### We built a software factory in 10 days. Here's what we learned. [...] Escalated to human review. One or more criteria are not met, or the agent flagged something worth a human look. The comment explains why and a label is added for tracking.

Auto-approve policy flow diagram

Every PR is reviewed by the AI agent. Low-risk PRs are approved automatically. All others are escalated. A human always merges.

### Governance

The AI agent can approve the review, but a person always clicks the merge button. That merge is the traceable approval event for SOC 2: the agent handles the review workload, the human controls what ships. The agent's review comment stays in version control alongside the merging engineer's identity and timestamp. [...] 1. Fewer than 1,000 lines changed (additions and deletions combined)
2. No protobuf changes added or modified
3. No database migrations added or modified
4. No infrastructure or CI configuration changes
5. No authentication or authorization logic changes
6. No audit logging or monitoring changes

If any single criterion is not met, the change is routed to human review.

### How the review works

When a pull request is opened, the AI agent reviews it in an isolated environment with independent context. It evaluates the change against the low-risk criteria and code quality, then posts a structured comment:

Approved. The change meets all low-risk criteria. The comment explains the reasoning for each criterion.
